records.source: Ἰούδας Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ δοῦλος, ἀδελφὸς δὲ Ἰακώβου, τοῖς ἐν θεῷ πατρὶ ἠγαπημένοις καὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ τετηρημένοις κλητοῖς·
records.gloss: Jude, of Jesus Christ slave, brother but of James, to the [ones] in God [the] Father having been loved and for Jesus Christ having been kept, called;
pieces: From Jude, a servant of Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} and a brother of James, to those who have been called, who are loved by God the Father and kept safe for Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

L.1: Jude, a slave of Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} and brother of James, to the called, loved in God [the] Father and kept for Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.1: This letter is from Jude. I am a servant of Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, and I am a brother of James. I am writing to you whom God has called. God the Father loves you, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is keeping you safe for Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: Jude: most likely the brother of James, the leader of the Jerusalem church, and so also a brother of Jesus
alternatives: the apostle called Judas of James (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13)
decisions.reason: The Greek name is Ἰούδας, the same name as Judas Iscariot and as Judah in the Old Testament. Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3 name a James and a Judas among the brothers of Jesus, and a James called the Lord's brother led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). A writer who needed to say no more than "brother of James" was most likely pointing to that well-known James, which would make Jude a brother of Jesus as well. He does not claim that tie: he calls himself a slave of Jesus Christ. The New Testament names other men called Judas, among them an apostle, "Judas of James" (Luke 6:16), but Jude does not call himself an apostle and speaks of the apostles as others (verse 17).

decisions.choice: slave: someone owned by a master and wholly at his service
decisions.reason: δοῦλος is the ordinary word for a slave, a person who belongs to another. To call oneself a slave of Jesus Christ is to say that one belongs to him and serves him alone, as Paul, James and Peter also say of themselves (Romans 1:1; James 1:1; 2 Peter 1:1). Verse 4 calls Jesus Christ "our only Master", the word for a slave's owner.

decisions.choice: the called: the readers, described as loved and kept
decisions.reason: The last word, κλητοῖς, "called", is the word the article τοῖς belongs to; "loved" and "kept" are perfect participles that describe the called. The perfect tense speaks of a state that began in the past and continues: loved and still loved, kept and still kept. God's calling, love and keeping frame the letter, here and again in verses 21 and 24.

decisions.choice: loved in God the Father: loved by God and held within his love
alternatives: loved in the sphere of God the Father, as people who belong to him
decisions.reason: The phrase is unusual, with "in" rather than "by". It most likely means that they are loved by God and remain within that love; verse 21 tells them to keep themselves in God's love.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "loved"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads ἠγαπημένοις, "having been loved", the reading of the oldest manuscripts. Many later manuscripts read a word meaning "sanctified", and the King James Version follows them ("sanctified by God the Father"). "Loved in God" is an unusual phrase, and a copyist may have changed it to the more familiar "sanctified" (compare 1 Corinthians 1:2). Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: kept for Jesus Christ: guarded by God for the day when Jesus Christ comes
decisions.reason: Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ has no preposition. The dative case most naturally means "for" here (kept for him); it can also mean "by" (kept by him). The passive points to God as the one who keeps, the one who "is able to guard you" (verse 24). The verb τηρέω runs through the letter: the angels did not keep their position and are kept for judgment (verse 6), darkness is kept for the false teachers (verse 13), and the readers are told to keep themselves in God's love (verse 21).

decisions.choice: Jude
decisions.reason: English Bibles have long called the writer of this letter Jude, which keeps him distinct from Judas Iscariot. In Greek the two names are the same (m1).

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m2) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

decisions.choice: Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Christ is the Greek for Messiah, the anointed king Israel was waiting for; the reader's setting chooses which word is shown.

decisions.choice: kept safe (B, R); whom God has called; God the Father ... is keeping you safe (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "kept safe", since "kept" alone could suggest being held back. Readable names God as the one who calls and keeps, as the passive voice implies (m6; compare verse 24).

records.heading: Greeting

records.source: ἔλεος ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη καὶ ἀγάπη πληθυνθείη.
records.gloss: Mercy to you and peace and love may it be multiplied.
pieces: May mercy, peace, and love be yours in ever greater measure.

L.2: Mercy to you and peace and love be multiplied.

R.2: I pray that you will have more and more mercy, peace, and love.

decisions.choice: a prayer: may mercy, peace and love be multiplied to you
decisions.reason: πληθυνθείη is a wish (the optative mood): may they be multiplied, given in greater and greater measure. 1 Peter 1:2 and 2 Peter 1:2 open with the same wish for grace and peace.

decisions.choice: mercy, peace, love: God's compassion, the wholeness he gives, and his love
decisions.reason: Most New Testament letters greet the readers with grace and peace. Jude names three gifts instead: mercy, peace and love. Love picks up "loved" in verse 1, and mercy returns in verses 21-23. All three come from God, the one in whom the readers are loved (verse 1).

decisions.choice: May mercy, peace, and love be yours in ever greater measure (B); I pray that you will have more and more (R)
alternatives: Mercy to you and peace and love be multiplied
decisions.reason: "Be multiplied" is not how English speaks of gifts. Balanced and Readable say the same wish in current English, as 2 Peter 1:2 does.

records.source: Ἀγαπητοί, πᾶσαν σπουδὴν ποιούμενος γράφειν ὑμῖν περὶ τῆς κοινῆς ἡμῶν σωτηρίας ἀνάγκην ἔσχον γράψαι ὑμῖν παρακαλῶν ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι τῇ ἅπαξ παραδοθείσῃ τοῖς ἁγίοις πίστει.
records.gloss: Beloved, all diligence making to write to you about the common of us salvation, necessity I had to write to you, urging [you] to contend for the once for all having been handed over to the saints faith.
pieces: Dear friends, I was doing all I could to write to you about the salvation we hold in common, but I found I had to write and urge you to fight hard for the faith that was handed over to God's holy people once for all.

L.3: Beloved, while making every effort to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write to you, urging [you] to contend for the faith that was handed over once for all to the saints.

R.3: Dear friends, I was working hard to write to you about the salvation that all of us share. But I have had to write to you about something else. I am urging you to stand up and fight for the faith. This faith was handed over to God's holy people once, for all time.

decisions.choice: beloved: people Jude loves, and whom God loves
decisions.reason: Ἀγαπητοί is used in letters for dear fellow believers (1 John 2:7; 2 Peter 3:1). It echoes verse 1, where the readers are loved by God. Jude uses it three times (verses 3, 17, 20), each time to turn from the false teachers to his readers.

decisions.choice: two kinds of writing: the letter he was eager to write about salvation, and the urgent appeal he found he had to write instead
alternatives: one letter: he was eager to write, and felt it necessary to do so as an appeal
decisions.reason: The present infinitive γράφειν, "to write", and the aorist γράψαι, "to write", stand side by side: he was busy with one kind of letter when a pressing need made him write this one. Verse 4 gives the need: false teachers have slipped in.

decisions.choice: our common salvation: the salvation all believers share, Jude and his readers alike
decisions.reason: κοινῆς means shared or held in common (Titus 1:4 speaks of "a common faith"). The salvation Jude meant to write about belongs to all of them equally.

decisions.choice: contend: struggle hard on behalf of something, as an athlete strains in a contest
decisions.reason: ἐπαγωνίζομαι is found only here in the New Testament. It is built on the word for a contest or a struggle, with a prefix that points to what the struggle is for. The readers are to strive for the faith; verses 20-23 show that this means building themselves up, praying and rescuing others, not only arguing.

decisions.choice: the faith handed over once for all to the saints: the truth that is believed, given to God's people once and complete
decisions.reason: Here πίστει is the faith that is believed, the content of the message, rather than the act of trusting (compare verse 20, "your most holy faith"). παραδοθείσῃ is the verb for handing on a teaching or tradition (1 Corinthians 11:2; 15:3; 2 Peter 2:21). ἅπαξ, "once for all", means it was given once and needs nothing added; the same word is in verse 5. The saints, or holy ones, are God's people.

decisions.choice: Dear friends
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "beloved"; Balanced and Readable say "dear friends", as in 1 John and 2 Peter, since "beloved" is no longer an ordinary way to address people.

decisions.choice: contend for (L); fight hard for (B); stand up and fight for (R)
decisions.reason: The word speaks of a hard struggle (m4). "Contend" keeps the sense at Literal; Balanced and Readable use plainer words for the same effort.

decisions.choice: the saints (L); God's holy people (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Saints" now suggests especially holy individuals. Balanced and Readable say what the word means here: all of God's people, as in Colossians.

decisions.choice: I have had to write to you about something else
alternatives: I had to write to you
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit the change of subject that the two infinitives imply (m2).

records.heading: Fight for the faith

records.source: παρεισέδυσαν γάρ τινες ἄνθρωποι, οἱ πάλαι προγεγραμμένοι εἰς τοῦτο τὸ κρίμα, ἀσεβεῖς, τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν χάριτα μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν καὶ τὸν μόνον δεσπότην καὶ κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἀρνούμενοι.
records.gloss: Slipped in for certain people, the [ones] long ago having been written beforehand for this the judgment, ungodly [ones], the of the God of us grace changing into sensuality and the only Master and Lord of us Jesus Christ denying.
pieces: For some {{gender:people|men}} have slipped in among you without being noticed. Long ago it was written that they would face this judgment. They are ungodly people who twist our God's grace into an excuse for shameless living, and who disown Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, our only Master and Lord.

L.4: For certain {{gender:people|men}} have slipped in, who long ago were written about beforehand for this judgment, ungodly [people], changing our God's grace into sensuality and denying our only Master and Lord, Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.4: I say this because some {{gender:people|men}} have sneaked in among you without anyone noticing. Long ago it was written that people like them would be judged. They do not honor God. They take our God's grace and use it as an excuse to live shamelessly. And they turn against Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, who alone is our Master and Lord.

decisions.choice: slipped in: came in secretly, unnoticed
decisions.reason: παρεισδύω means to slip in alongside, without being noticed. Galatians 2:4 uses a similar picture, and 2 Peter 2:1 a related verb. γάρ, "for", gives the reason for the appeal in verse 3. These people are inside the church and share its meals (verse 12).

decisions.choice: long ago written about beforehand for this judgment: the judgment on such people was set down in writing long before they came
alternatives: long ago appointed (or designated) for this condemnation
decisions.reason: προγράφω means to write beforehand (Romans 15:4) or to post a public notice (Galatians 3:1). With πάλαι, "long ago", the first sense is most likely. Jude goes on to show where it was written: the examples from Israel's Scriptures (verses 5-7 and 11), the prophecy of Enoch (verses 14-15) and the apostles' warning (verses 17-18). "This judgment" points ahead to those passages. The text speaks of the judgment that awaits them; it does not say how they came to be what they are.

decisions.choice: ungodly: people who live without reverence for God
decisions.reason: ἀσεβής and its related words come six times in Jude, four of them in the prophecy of verse 15 and once more in verse 18. They describe people who treat God without reverence, and it shows in what they do.

decisions.choice: changing God's grace into sensuality: treating God's free kindness as permission for unrestrained living
decisions.reason: μετατίθημι means to change something or move it to another use. ἀσέλγεια is open, unrestrained indulgence, especially sexual, that does not care who sees it (as in 2 Peter 2:2, 7, 18). They take God's grace, his undeserved favor that forgives, and make it a reason to sin freely, the error Paul answers in Romans 6:1-2.

decisions.choice: our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ: one person, Jesus Christ, called both Master and Lord
alternatives: two persons: the only Master (God), and our Lord Jesus Christ
decisions.reason: One article, τὸν, governs both nouns, δεσπότην and κύριον, and "our" and the name Jesus Christ follow them, so the natural reading is one person with two titles, as in 2 Peter 1:1, "our God and Savior Jesus Christ". δεσπότης is the word for a slave's owner. It is used of God (Luke 2:29; Acts 4:24; Revelation 6:10) and of Christ in 2 Peter 2:1, "the Master who bought them", the parallel to this verse. "Only" recalls the confession that the LORD alone is God (Deuteronomy 6:4); here it is said of Jesus Christ.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "the only Master"
alternatives: "the only Master, God, and our Lord Jesus Christ"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "God" after "Master", and the King James Version follows them ("the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ"). With that word the verse reads more easily as naming two persons. The earlier manuscripts do not have it. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: denying: disowning him, above all by how they live
decisions.reason: ἀρνέομαι means to say no to someone, to disown them. Nothing in Jude says that they denied Christ in words; their unrestrained, ungodly life rejects his rule (compare Titus 1:16). Verse 8 says the same in other words: they reject lordship.

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: ἄνθρωποι means human beings, and the text does not say whether women were among them. "People" is the default; "men" is the traditional form.

decisions.choice: sensuality (L); an excuse for shameless living (B); an excuse to live shamelessly (R)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Peter 2, Literal says "sensuality" and Balanced and Readable describe the behavior as shameless (m4). "An excuse for" says in plain words what turning grace into sensuality means.

decisions.choice: disown (B); turn against (R)
decisions.reason: "Deny" in current English usually means to say something is not true. Balanced and Readable use words for rejecting a person, as in 2 Peter 2:1 (m7).

decisions.choice: They do not honor God
decisions.reason: Readable says what "ungodly" means, as in 2 Peter 2 (m3).

records.source: Ὑπομνῆσαι δὲ ὑμᾶς βούλομαι, εἰδότας ὑμᾶς ἅπαξ πάντα, ὅτι Ἰησοῦς λαὸν ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου σώσας τὸ δεύτερον τοὺς μὴ πιστεύσαντας ἀπώλεσεν, ἀγγέλους τε τοὺς μὴ τηρήσαντας τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχὴν ἀλλὰ ἀπολιπόντας τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον εἰς κρίσιν μεγάλης ἡμέρας δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις ὑπὸ ζόφον τετήρηκεν·
records.gloss: To remind but you I want, knowing you once for all all things, that Jesus a people out of [the] land of Egypt having saved, the second [time] those not having believed destroyed, \v 6 angels and those not having kept the of themselves position but having deserted the own dwelling, for [the] judgment of [the] great day with bonds everlasting under gloom he has kept;
pieces: Now I want to remind you of something, though you know it all already. Jesus saved a people out of the land of Egypt, but afterward {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} destroyed those among them who did not believe.

And the angels who did not stay in the place of authority that was theirs, but abandoned their own dwelling, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has kept in everlasting chains in deepest darkness, ready for judgment when the great day comes.

L.5: But I want to remind you, though you know all things once for all, that Jesus, having saved a people out of the land of Egypt, the second time destroyed the ones who did not believe;
L.6: and angels who did not keep their own position but deserted their own dwelling {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has kept for [the] judgment of [the] great day in everlasting bonds under gloom.

R.5: You already know all this, but I want to remind you of it. Jesus saved the people of Israel and brought them out of the land of Egypt. But later {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} destroyed the ones who did not believe.
R.6: Remember the angels who did not stay in the place of authority God had given them. They left the home where they belonged. So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has kept them in the dark, in chains that will last forever. They are being held there until the great day of judgment.

decisions.choice: I want to remind you, though you know all things once for all: Jude tells them nothing new
decisions.reason: Ὑπομνῆσαι, "to remind", and εἰδότας, "knowing", say that what follows is what the readers have already been taught; Jude calls them to remember it, as 2 Peter 1:12-13 does. In the SBLGNT ἅπαξ, "once for all", goes with "knowing": they have been fully taught.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "Jesus"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads Ἰησοῦς, "Jesus", as the one who saved the people out of Egypt. The manuscripts differ here more than anywhere else in Jude. "Jesus" is the reading of some important early manuscripts, among them Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Vaticanus, and of some early translations. Others, among them Codex Sinaiticus and most later manuscripts, read "the Lord"; a few read "God"; and the early papyrus P72 has an unusual "God Christ". "Jesus" is the harder reading: it is easy to see why a copyist would change it to "the Lord" or "God", and hard to see why anyone would change those to "Jesus". That is the main reason for preferring it, but the evidence is divided, and "the Lord" is also well supported. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: Jesus as the one who saved Israel from Egypt: Jude speaks of Jesus as present and acting in Israel's history
alternatives: Joshua, whose name is the same in Greek
decisions.reason: If "Jesus" is the original reading (m2), Jude places Jesus Christ, his only Master and Lord (verse 4), in Israel's past: he saved the people out of Egypt, later judged them, and keeps the rebel angels for judgment (verse 6). Paul writes in a similar way when he says that the rock that followed Israel was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). The reading does not mean that the name Jesus was known in Moses' day, and it does not deny that the LORD, Israel's God, brought them out; it says that the one Christians call Jesus was at work there. In Greek Ἰησοῦς is also the name Joshua, but Joshua did not bring the people out of Egypt, destroy the unbelievers or keep angels for judgment, so that reading is unlikely. With "the Lord" the verse would leave open whether God or Christ is meant.

decisions.choice: saved out of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe: the exodus, and the generation that died in the wilderness
decisions.reason: The people were brought out of Egypt (Exodus 12-14), but when they refused to trust God and enter the land, that generation died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:11, 26-35; compare 1 Corinthians 10:1-5; Hebrews 3:16-19). τὸ δεύτερον, "the second time", most likely means afterward, the second act after the saving: being rescued once did not protect those who later refused to believe.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "once for all" goes with "knowing"
alternatives: "once" goes with "saved": "having once saved a people ... the second time destroyed"
decisions.reason: In the SBLGNT ἅπαξ stands before πάντα and goes with "knowing". Some manuscripts place it after the name, with "saved", which pairs "once" with "the second time". The meaning of the verse hardly changes. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: angels who did not keep their own position: most likely the angels of Genesis 6:1-4, as Jewish tradition told the story
alternatives: the first rebellion of angels against God, before the creation of humankind
decisions.reason: ἀρχὴν means a beginning, and so a rule or a position of authority; οἰκητήριον is a dwelling place (2 Corinthians 5:2). These angels left the rank and home God gave them. Jewish writings of the time, especially 1 Enoch 6-16, told Genesis 6:1-4 as the story of angels ("the sons of God") who left heaven to take human wives and who were bound in darkness until the judgment. Jude quotes 1 Enoch in verses 14-15, and verse 7 says that Sodom sinned "in the same way as these", which fits this story. The text itself names only their desertion and their punishment, as 2 Peter 2:4 does.

decisions.choice: did not keep ... has kept: a play on the same verb
decisions.reason: The angels did not keep (τηρήσαντας) their position, so they are kept (τετήρηκεν) in bonds. It is the verb of verse 1, where the readers are kept for Jesus Christ, and of verses 13 and 21. In the SBLGNT the subject is still the one named in verse 5.

decisions.choice: everlasting bonds under gloom, for the judgment of the great day: a prison of darkness that holds them until the final judgment
decisions.reason: ἀΐδιος means everlasting; it is a different word from the "eternal" of verses 7 and 21, though close in meaning. The bonds hold them until the judgment: the text speaks of where they are held now, as 2 Peter 2:4 does with "chains of gloom". ζόφος is deep, murky darkness, the word of verse 13 and of 2 Peter 2:4 and 17. "The great day" is the day of the Lord's judgment (Joel 2:31; Revelation 6:17).

decisions.choice: Jesus (all levels), with a footnote giving "the Lord" and "God"
decisions.reason: Every level renders the SBLGNT text (m2). The footnote lets readers see the other readings.

decisions.choice: everlasting bonds (L); everlasting chains (B); chains that will last forever (R)
decisions.reason: "Eternal" is kept for the different word in verses 7 and 21 (m8). Balanced and Readable say "chains", the ordinary English for bonds that hold a prisoner.

decisions.choice: deepest darkness (B); in the dark (R)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Peter 2:4, Literal says "gloom" and Balanced and Readable say plainly how dark the prison is.

decisions.choice: the people of Israel; the place of authority God had given them
decisions.reason: Readable names the people (m4) and says who gave the angels their place (m6), which the story assumes.

records.heading: Warnings from the past

records.source: ὡς Σόδομα καὶ Γόμορρα καὶ αἱ περὶ αὐτὰς πόλεις, τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις ἐκπορνεύσασαι καὶ ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας, πρόκεινται δεῖγμα πυρὸς αἰωνίου δίκην ὑπέχουσαι.
records.gloss: As Sodom and Gomorrah and the around them cities, the like manner to these having committed sexual immorality and having gone after flesh other, are set forth [as] an example, of fire eternal [the] penalty undergoing.
pieces: So too Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns around them, which, like those angels, gave themselves to sexual immorality and went after flesh of another kind, now lie before us as an example, suffering the penalty of eternal fire.

L.7: So too Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, having committed sexual immorality in the same way as these and having gone after other flesh, are set forth [as] an example, undergoing [the] penalty of eternal fire.

R.7: Think too of Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns around them. Like those angels, the people there were sexually immoral and went after flesh of a different kind. Their punishment by eternal fire is set before everyone as a warning.

decisions.choice: as: a third example, joined to the two in verses 5-6
decisions.reason: ὡς links Sodom and Gomorrah to what comes before: like the unbelieving people and the angels, these cities show what happens to those who rebel. The SBLGNT ends the previous sentence with a raised dot, and this record follows that division.

decisions.choice: Sodom, Gomorrah and the cities around them: destroyed by fire from heaven (Genesis 19:24-29)
decisions.reason: Genesis 19:24-29 tells how fire and sulfur fell on Sodom and Gomorrah; Deuteronomy 29:23 names two of the cities around them, Admah and Zeboiim. The Old Testament and the New hold them up again and again as the great example of judgment (Isaiah 1:9; Matthew 10:15; 2 Peter 2:6).

decisions.choice: in the same way as these: most likely as the angels of verse 6
alternatives: as Sodom and Gomorrah themselves: the cities around sinned as those two did
as the false teachers, who are "these" in verse 8
decisions.reason: τούτοις is masculine or neuter, not feminine like the cities (πόλεις) and the participles that describe them. It most likely points back to the angels of verse 6, the nearest masculine plural. Read that way, Sodom sinned in the same way as the angels: both crossed the boundary between heavenly beings and human beings. Some take it of Sodom and Gomorrah, whose names are neuter in Greek, or of the false teachers.

decisions.choice: went after other flesh: pursued sexual relations outside the bounds God set; the text says "other" or "different" flesh and does not say more
alternatives: sexual relations with angels: the men of Sodom demanded the visitors, who were angels (Genesis 19:1-11)
decisions.reason: ἐκπορνεύω is a strong word for sexual immorality. ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας is literally "after other flesh" or "different flesh". In Genesis 19:1-11 the men of Sodom demanded to have sex with Lot's guests, who were angels, though the men did not know it. If verse 7 compares Sodom with the angels of verse 6 (m3), the point is that both reached across the boundary between angels and humans. Others read "other flesh" as flesh other than what is natural or proper, and so take it of same-sex relations, or of sexual perversion in general; the men of Sodom were demanding sex with other men. Ezekiel 16:49-50 also names Sodom's pride and its neglect of the poor. Jude says that the cities committed sexual immorality and went after "other flesh"; he does not describe the act further.

decisions.choice: set forth as an example, undergoing the penalty of eternal fire
alternatives: an example of eternal fire, undergoing punishment
decisions.reason: πυρὸς αἰωνίου, "of eternal fire", can go with "penalty" (the penalty of eternal fire) or with "example" (an example of eternal fire). Either way the destroyed cities stand as a public warning of the judgment of fire that does not end (2 Peter 2:6). δίκην is a penalty handed down by a judge.

decisions.choice: other flesh (L); flesh of another kind (B); flesh of a different kind (R)
decisions.reason: All three levels keep Jude's own expression and do not choose among the readings (m4).

decisions.choice: like those angels
alternatives: in the same way as these
decisions.reason: "These" has no clear antecedent in English. Balanced and Readable name the angels, the most likely sense (m3).

decisions.choice: set before everyone as a warning
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of example the cities are: a warning of judgment (m5).

records.source: Ὁμοίως μέντοι καὶ οὗτοι ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι σάρκα μὲν μιαίνουσιν, κυριότητα δὲ ἀθετοῦσιν, δόξας δὲ βλασφημοῦσιν.
records.gloss: Likewise yet also these dreaming [ones] [the] flesh on one hand defile, lordship and reject, glorious [ones] and blaspheme.
pieces: Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject the Lord's authority, and slander the glorious ones.

L.8: Yet in the same way these also, dreaming, defile the flesh, reject lordship, and blaspheme glorious ones.

R.8: These dreamers act in the same way. They make their own bodies unclean with sin. They reject the Lord's authority. And they insult glorious beings in the heavenly world.

decisions.choice: likewise: the false teachers do what the people of verses 5-7 did
decisions.reason: Ὁμοίως, "likewise", with μέντοι, "yet", says that in spite of those warnings these people do the same things: they defile the flesh like Sodom, reject authority like the angels who left their place, and speak against heavenly beings. οὗτοι, "these", is Jude's word for the false teachers through the rest of the letter (verses 10, 12, 16, 19).

decisions.choice: dreaming: they claim visions in dreams as the authority for what they do
alternatives: they live in a dream world, deluded
decisions.reason: ἐνυπνιάζομαι is used of dreams that bring visions (Acts 2:17, quoting Joel 2:28). The Law warns against a prophet or "dreamer of dreams" who leads people away from God (Deuteronomy 13:1-5), and the Greek Old Testament uses this verb there. Jude probably means that they appeal to their own dreams or visions to justify what they do; the word may also describe them as people out of touch with what is real.

decisions.choice: defile the flesh: make their bodies unclean by sexual sin
decisions.reason: The words recall Sodom in verse 7. "Flesh" here is their own body; they defile it by the sexual immorality Jude has described.

decisions.choice: lordship: the Lord's authority
alternatives: angelic powers (the "glorious ones" of the next words)
decisions.reason: κυριότητα comes from the word for lord. Since the false teachers deny "our only Master and Lord" (verse 4), the most likely sense is that they reject the Lord's rule over them. In Ephesians 1:21 and Colossians 1:16 the same word names a rank of spiritual powers, and the next words speak of heavenly beings, so some read it that way. 2 Peter 2:10 has the same pair of ideas.

decisions.choice: glorious ones: heavenly beings, most likely including fallen angels
decisions.reason: δόξας ("glories") is used for angelic beings in Jewish writing, and 2 Peter 2:10 uses it the same way. Verse 9 gives the example: even the archangel Michael did not speak abusively to the devil. So the beings these people mock probably include evil powers, whom they treat with contempt they have no right to.

decisions.choice: blaspheme (L); slander (B); insult (R)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Peter 2:10, Literal keeps the Greek word. In current English "blaspheme" is used only of speech against God, so Balanced and Readable use words for abusive speech against others.

decisions.choice: the Lord's authority
decisions.reason: "Lordship" alone is unclear in English; Balanced and Readable say whose authority, as in 2 Peter 2:10 (m4).

decisions.choice: the flesh (L); their bodies (B); their own bodies (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what flesh means here (m3).

decisions.choice: glorious beings in the heavenly world
decisions.reason: Readable says who the glorious ones are, as in 2 Peter 2:10 (m5).

records.heading: What these dreamers are like

records.source: ὁ δὲ Μιχαὴλ ὁ ἀρχάγγελος, ὅτε τῷ διαβόλῳ διακρινόμενος διελέγετο περὶ τοῦ Μωϋσέως σώματος, οὐκ ἐτόλμησεν κρίσιν ἐπενεγκεῖν βλασφημίας, ἀλλὰ εἶπεν· Ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι κύριος.
records.gloss: But Michael the archangel, when with the devil disputing he was arguing about the of Moses body, not did dare a judgment to bring of blasphemy, but said: May rebuke you [the] Lord.
pieces: But when Michael, the archangel, was in a dispute with the devil, arguing over the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him. Instead he said, "May the Lord rebuke you."

L.9: But Michael the archangel, when he was disputing with the devil and arguing about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring against [him] a blasphemous judgment, but said, "[The] Lord rebuke you."

R.9: But think of Michael, the chief angel. He was arguing with the devil about the body of Moses. Yet he did not dare to insult the devil when he accused him. He only said, "May the Lord rebuke you!"

decisions.choice: Michael the archangel: a chief angel, named in Daniel as a protector of Israel
decisions.reason: ἀρχάγγελος means chief angel; the word is used elsewhere in the New Testament only in 1 Thessalonians 4:16. Michael is named in Daniel 10:13, 21 and 12:1 as a great prince who stands for God's people, and in Revelation 12:7 he fights against the dragon.

decisions.choice: the dispute over the body of Moses: a story not found in the Old Testament, which early Christian writers say came from a book called the Assumption of Moses
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 34:5-6 says that Moses died in Moab and was buried there, and that no one knows the place of his grave. The Old Testament says nothing of a dispute between Michael and the devil. Several early Christian writers, among them Clement of Alexandria and Origen, say that Jude took this story from a Jewish book known as the Assumption of Moses. A Jewish work about Moses' last words, usually called the Testament of Moses, survives in one incomplete Latin manuscript; its ending is lost, and the part that survives does not contain the dispute. Whether that work and the Assumption were one book is not certain. Jude tells a story his readers knew; he does not name his source.

decisions.choice: a blasphemous judgment: a condemnation spoken with insult
alternatives: a judgment for blasphemy: he did not pass sentence on the devil's own slander
decisions.reason: κρίσιν ἐπενεγκεῖν βλασφημίας is literally "a judgment of blasphemy". Most likely it means an abusive verdict, an accusation made with insulting words. Michael, though a chief angel, left the verdict to God. The point for Jude's readers is verse 8: the false teachers speak with contempt about heavenly beings, which even Michael did not do to the devil. 2 Peter 2:11 makes the same point without the story.

decisions.choice: The Lord rebuke you: the words spoken to Satan in Zechariah 3:2
decisions.reason: In Zechariah's vision, Satan stands to accuse Joshua the high priest, and the angel of the LORD says, "The LORD rebuke you, Satan." The Hebrew there has the divine name; Jude's Greek has κύριος, "Lord". Ἐπιτιμήσαι is a wish (the optative mood): may the Lord rebuke you. Zechariah 3 comes back in verse 23.

decisions.choice: a blasphemous judgment (L); a slanderous judgment (B); insult ... when he accused him (R)
decisions.reason: The same choice as in verse 8 and 2 Peter 2:11: Literal keeps "blasphemous"; Balanced and Readable use words for abusive speech (m3).

decisions.choice: the chief angel
decisions.reason: Readable says what "archangel" means (m1).

records.source: οὗτοι δὲ ὅσα μὲν οὐκ οἴδασιν βλασφημοῦσιν, ὅσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα ἐπίστανται, ἐν τούτοις φθείρονται.
records.gloss: These but, whatever on one hand not they know they blaspheme, whatever but by nature as the irrational animals they understand, in these they are destroyed.
pieces: But these people slander what they know nothing about, while the things they know by instinct, like animals without reason, are the very things that destroy them.

L.10: But these [people] blaspheme the things they do not know; and the things they understand naturally, like irrational animals, in these they are destroyed.

R.10: But these people insult things they know nothing about. They are like wild animals that cannot think. The only things they understand are the things they know by instinct, and those are the very things that destroy them.

decisions.choice: two kinds of things: what they do not know, and what they know only by instinct
decisions.reason: μὲν and δὲ set two clauses side by side. What they do not know is the spiritual world, the glorious beings of verse 8; what they know by instinct, φυσικῶς, "naturally", like animals, is the life of bodily appetite. They mock the first and are ruined by the second.

decisions.choice: they are destroyed: ruined by the very appetites they follow
decisions.reason: φθείρω can mean to corrupt or to destroy. The parallel in 2 Peter 2:12 says that like animals they will be destroyed, and the examples in verses 5-7 end in destruction, so ruin is most likely meant here.

decisions.choice: a parallel to 2 Peter 2:12
decisions.reason: 2 Peter 2:12 says the same: like irrational animals, born for capture and destruction, they slander what they do not understand and will be destroyed.

decisions.choice: blaspheme (L); slander (B); insult (R)
decisions.reason: The same choice as in verse 8.

decisions.choice: irrational animals (L); animals without reason (B); wild animals that cannot think (R)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Peter 2:12.

records.source: οὐαὶ αὐτοῖς, ὅτι τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ Κάϊν ἐπορεύθησαν, καὶ τῇ πλάνῃ τοῦ Βαλαὰμ μισθοῦ ἐξεχύθησαν, καὶ τῇ ἀντιλογίᾳ τοῦ Κόρε ἀπώλοντο.
records.gloss: Woe to them, because in the way of the Cain they went, and to the error of the Balaam for wages they poured themselves out, and in the rebellion of the Korah they perished.
pieces: Woe to them! They have walked in the way of Cain. For the sake of pay they have thrown themselves into the error of Balaam. They have perished in the rebellion of Korah.

L.11: Woe to them, for they went in the way of Cain, and for wages they poured themselves out into the error of Balaam, and in the rebellion of Korah they perished.

R.11: How terrible it will be for them! They have lived like Cain, who killed his brother. They have rushed into the same wrong as Balaam, all for money. And they will be destroyed, just as Korah was when he rebelled against Moses.

decisions.choice: woe to them: a cry of grief and warning over people facing judgment
decisions.reason: οὐαὶ is the prophets' cry over those who face God's judgment (Isaiah 5:8-22; Habakkuk 2:6-19), and Jesus used it the same way (Matthew 23:13-29). It both mourns and warns.

decisions.choice: the way of Cain: the path of the man who killed his brother
decisions.reason: Cain killed his brother Abel after God had warned him that sin was waiting at his door (Genesis 4:1-16). 1 John 3:12 says Cain belonged to the evil one, and Hebrews 11:4 sets him against Abel's faith. To go in his way is to follow his path.

decisions.choice: the error of Balaam: the prophet who was willing to curse Israel for pay, and who led Israel into sin
decisions.reason: Balaam was hired to curse Israel (Numbers 22-24); afterward his advice led Israel into sexual sin and idolatry at Peor (Numbers 25:1-3; 31:16; compare Revelation 2:14). 2 Peter 2:15 says he "loved the wage of wrongdoing". ἐξεχύθησαν, "they poured themselves out", pictures people rushing headlong into his error for the sake of gain (μισθοῦ).

decisions.choice: the rebellion of Korah: the uprising against Moses and Aaron that ended when the ground swallowed the rebels
decisions.reason: Korah led a revolt against the leadership God had given through Moses and Aaron, and he and his followers perished (Numbers 16:1-35). ἀντιλογίᾳ means speaking against, and so rebellion.

decisions.choice: three past tenses: their end is spoken of as already settled
decisions.reason: The three verbs are aorists, the tense of a completed act. The first two describe what they have done. The third, ἀπώλοντο, "they perished", speaks of their destruction as if it had already happened, because it is as certain as Korah's.

decisions.choice: How terrible it will be for them
decisions.reason: "Woe" is no longer ordinary English. Literal and Balanced keep the prophets' cry; Readable says what it means (m1).

decisions.choice: who killed his brother; all for money; when he rebelled against Moses
decisions.reason: Readable reminds the reader who the three men were (m2-m4).

decisions.choice: they perished (L); they have perished (B); they will be destroyed, just as Korah was (R)
decisions.reason: All three levels say that their end is certain (m5); Readable says it as a future, which is what the past tense means here.

records.source: οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ ἐν ταῖς ἀγάπαις ὑμῶν σπιλάδες συνευωχούμενοι, ἀφόβως ἑαυτοὺς ποιμαίνοντες, νεφέλαι ἄνυδροι ὑπὸ ἀνέμων παραφερόμεναι, δένδρα φθινοπωρινὰ ἄκαρπα δὶς ἀποθανόντα ἐκριζωθέντα, κύματα ἄγρια θαλάσσης ἐπαφρίζοντα τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας, ἀστέρες πλανῆται οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς αἰῶνα τετήρηται.
records.gloss: These are the [ones] in the love feasts of you reefs, feasting together fearlessly, themselves shepherding, clouds waterless by winds being carried along, trees late-autumn fruitless, twice having died, having been uprooted, \v 13 waves wild of [the] sea foaming up the of themselves shames, stars wandering, for whom the gloom of the darkness to [the] age has been kept.
pieces: At your love feasts these people are like reefs hidden under the water. They eat with you without a trace of fear, shepherds who look after only themselves. They are clouds that bring no rain, blown along by the winds; trees in late autumn with no fruit, twice dead and pulled up by the roots;
wild waves of the sea, churning up their shameful deeds like foam; wandering stars, for whom the blackest darkness has been kept forever.

L.12: These are the ones [who are] reefs in your love feasts, feasting together fearlessly, shepherding themselves; clouds without water, carried along by winds; trees of late autumn, fruitless, twice dead, uprooted;
L.13: wild waves of [the] sea, foaming up their own shames; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever.

R.12: These people are like hidden rocks under the water that wreck ships. They are there at your love feasts, the meals where you eat together. They eat with you and are not afraid of anything. They take care of no one but themselves. They are like clouds that bring no rain and are blown along by the wind. They are like trees at the end of autumn that have no fruit. They are dead twice over, pulled out roots and all.
R.13: They are like wild waves in the sea, throwing up their shameful deeds like foam. They are like stars that wander off course. A place of deep darkness is being kept ready for them forever.

decisions.choice: reefs: rocks hidden under the surface, on which ships are wrecked
decisions.reason: σπιλάς normally means a rock in or under the sea, a reef. A word that sounds much the same, σπίλος, means a stain or spot, and 2 Peter 2:13, the parallel verse, calls the false teachers "stains and blemishes". Some read Jude's word in that sense too, but the usual meaning gives a clear picture: like rocks hidden under calm water, these people make the church's meals dangerous for anyone who comes near.

decisions.choice: love feasts: the church's shared meals
decisions.reason: ἀγάπαις is the plural of the word for love. Here it names the common meals of the early churches, which could include the Lord's Supper (Acts 2:46; 1 Corinthians 11:20-34). συνευωχούμενοι, "feasting together", is the word 2 Peter 2:13 uses. The false teachers were not outsiders; they sat at the same table.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "love feasts"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads ἀγάπαις, "love feasts". Some manuscripts read a word that differs by a few letters and means "deceptions". In 2 Peter 2:13 the situation is reversed: the SBLGNT reads "deceptions" there, and some manuscripts read "love feasts". Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: shepherding themselves: leaders who care only for themselves
decisions.reason: Ezekiel 34:2-10 condemns the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves instead of the flock. ἀφόβως, "fearlessly", means without reverence for God or without shame.

decisions.choice: four pictures from nature: they promise much and give nothing, and their end is ruin
decisions.reason: Clouds that bring no rain promise what they never give (Proverbs 25:14). Trees in late autumn, the time of harvest, should have fruit and have none. Wild waves throw foam and refuse onto the shore; Isaiah 57:20 compares the wicked to the tossing sea, whose waters cast up mire and mud. Wandering stars leave their proper course; 1 Enoch 18:13-16 and 21:1-6 describe stars bound in punishment for not keeping their appointed times, and that may be Jude's background, as 1 Enoch is in verses 6 and 14. The pictures move through air, earth, sea and sky.

decisions.choice: twice dead, uprooted: dead because fruitless, and dead again because pulled up, beyond any hope of growth
alternatives: dead in this life and dead in the judgment (the second death, Revelation 20:14)
decisions.reason: δὶς, "twice", is not explained. Most likely the tree is dead once in bearing no fruit and dead again in being uprooted. Some see a reference to the second death of Revelation 20:14.

decisions.choice: the gloom of darkness kept forever: the place of punishment, already reserved for them
decisions.reason: 2 Peter 2:17 has the same words, without "forever". The verb is the "keep" of verses 1, 6 and 21: the darkness is kept for them as the readers are kept for Jesus Christ.

decisions.choice: reefs (L); reefs hidden under the water (B); hidden rocks under the water that wreck ships (R)
decisions.reason: Literal gives the word; Balanced and Readable explain the danger it pictures (m1).

decisions.choice: the meals where you eat together
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a love feast was (m2).

decisions.choice: like (B, R)
decisions.reason: The pictures are metaphors. Balanced adds "like" for the first picture; Readable adds it for each, which makes clear that they are comparisons.

decisions.choice: the blackest darkness (B); a place of deep darkness (R)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Peter 2:17 (m7).

records.source: Προεφήτευσεν δὲ καὶ τούτοις ἕβδομος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ Ἑνὼχ λέγων· Ἰδοὺ ἦλθεν κύριος ἐν ἁγίαις μυριάσιν αὐτοῦ, ποιῆσαι κρίσιν κατὰ πάντων καὶ ἐλέγξαι πάντας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς περὶ πάντων τῶν ἔργων ἀσεβείας αὐτῶν ὧν ἠσέβησαν καὶ περὶ πάντων τῶν σκληρῶν ὧν ἐλάλησαν κατ’ αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀσεβεῖς.
records.gloss: Prophesied and also to these [the] seventh from Adam Enoch, saying: Look, came [the] Lord with holy myriads of him, \v 15 to do judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly concerning all the works of ungodliness of them which they did ungodly and concerning all the hard [things] which spoke against him sinners ungodly.
pieces: Enoch, the seventh in line from Adam, also prophesied about these people. He said, "Look! The Lord is coming with tens of thousands of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy ones

to bring judgment on everyone, and to prove all the ungodly guilty of every ungodly deed they have done in their ungodliness, and of every hard word spoken against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} by ungodly sinners."

L.14: And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about these, saying, "Look, [the] Lord came with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy myriads,
L.15: to execute judgment against all, and to convict all the ungodly concerning all their works of ungodliness that they did in ungodliness, and concerning all the hard words that ungodly sinners spoke against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

R.14: Enoch was the seventh in the family line that began with Adam. He also spoke a prophecy about these people. He said, "Look! The Lord will come with many thousands of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy angels.
R.15: He will judge everyone. He will show that all the ungodly are guilty of all the ungodly things they have done. And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will show that they are guilty of all the hard and cruel words that ungodly sinners have said against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: Enoch, the seventh from Adam: the Enoch of Genesis 5, seventh in the line from Adam, counting Adam as the first
decisions.reason: Genesis 5:3-24 gives the line Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch: counting Adam, Enoch is the seventh. Genesis 5:24 says that Enoch walked with God, and then he was not there, because God took him. The description also keeps him distinct from Cain's son Enoch (Genesis 4:17). 1 Enoch 60:8 calls him "the seventh from Adam" in the same way.

decisions.choice: a quotation of 1 Enoch 1:9
decisions.reason: Jude's words are a close quotation of 1 Enoch 1:9. 1 Enoch is a Jewish writing, made up of several parts written in the last centuries before Christ, that tells of visions given to Enoch. It is not in the Hebrew Bible, nor in the Old Testament of most Christian churches, though the Ethiopian Orthodox Church includes it in its canon. It survives complete only in Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia; parts survive in Greek, and fragments in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jude says that Enoch prophesied, and he applies the prophecy to the false teachers. The text says nothing about the status of the book as a whole: it does not call it Scripture, and it does not say that it is not.

decisions.choice: came: a past tense used in prophecy for a future event, seen as already certain
decisions.reason: ἦλθεν is an aorist, normally a past tense. In a prophecy it presents the coming judgment as if it had already happened, because it is certain, as "they perished" does in verse 11. From Enoch's day it lay in the future, and from Jude's it is still to come.

decisions.choice: the Lord: in 1 Enoch, God; as Jude uses the prophecy, quite possibly the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: In 1 Enoch the one who comes with his holy ones is God himself, "the Holy Great One" (1 Enoch 1:3-9). Jude's quotation names him κύριος, "Lord". Jude uses that title for Jesus (verses 4, 17, 21, 25), and the New Testament speaks of the Lord Jesus coming with his holy ones (1 Thessalonians 3:13; Matthew 25:31), so Jude may apply the prophecy to him; but "Lord" is also used of God (verse 9), and the text does not say which.

decisions.choice: his holy myriads: tens of thousands of holy ones, his angels
decisions.reason: μυριάσιν means ten thousands, a countless host. The holy ones are the angels who come with the Lord at his judgment (Deuteronomy 33:2; Zechariah 14:5; Matthew 25:31).

decisions.choice: convict: prove guilty and expose; the repeated "ungodly" is the point of the prophecy
decisions.reason: ἐλέγχω means to prove someone guilty and expose their wrong. The prophecy uses the word for ungodliness four times: the ungodly, their works of ungodliness, which they did in ungodliness, ungodly sinners. The repetition is the point: their whole life is set against God. "Hard things" (σκληρῶν) are harsh, defiant words spoken against God, which verse 16 goes on to describe.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "all the ungodly"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads πάντας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς, "all the ungodly". Some early manuscripts, among them the papyrus P72 and Codex Sinaiticus, read "every soul" instead. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: came (L); is coming (B); will come (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the past tense; Balanced and Readable say what it means here, a sure future event (m3). All three describe the same coming.

decisions.choice: Look
decisions.reason: The style guide does not use "behold". "Look" calls for attention as the Greek word does.

decisions.choice: tens of thousands of his holy ones (B); many thousands of his holy angels (R)
decisions.reason: "Myriads" is not everyday English. Readable says who the holy ones are (m5).

decisions.choice: ungodly
alternatives: people who do not honor God
decisions.reason: Elsewhere Readable explains "ungodly" (verse 4), but here the word is repeated four times on purpose (m6), so Readable keeps it.

decisions.choice: the seventh in line from Adam (B); the seventh in the family line that began with Adam (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that the number counts generations (m1).

records.heading: Enoch's prophecy

records.source: οὗτοί εἰσιν γογγυσταί, μεμψίμοιροι, κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι, καὶ τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν λαλεῖ ὑπέρογκα, θαυμάζοντες πρόσωπα ὠφελείας χάριν.
records.gloss: These are grumblers, complainers about [their] lot, according to the desires of them going, and the mouth of them speaks swollen [things], admiring faces of advantage for the sake.
pieces: These people grumble and find fault with their lot in life. They live by their own desires. Their mouths speak big, boastful words, and they flatter people to get something out of them.

L.16: These are grumblers, complaining about their lot, going according to their desires; and their mouth speaks swollen [words], admiring faces for the sake of advantage.

R.16: These people are always grumbling and complaining that life is not fair to them. They do whatever they want. They brag with big words. And they flatter people to get what they want from them.

decisions.choice: grumblers: like Israel in the wilderness
decisions.reason: γογγυσταί recalls Israel's grumbling against God and Moses in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7-12; Numbers 14:27-29), which ended in the judgment of verse 5. Paul uses the same example (1 Corinthians 10:10).

decisions.choice: complaining about their lot: discontented with what God has given them
decisions.reason: μεμψίμοιροι describes someone who finds fault with his share in life. Their complaint is finally against God, who gives each person a lot.

decisions.choice: swollen words: boastful, arrogant talk
decisions.reason: ὑπέρογκα means puffed up, swollen beyond its size. 2 Peter 2:18 uses it of the false teachers' empty talk, and Daniel 11:36 says that the arrogant king will speak great things against God.

decisions.choice: admiring faces for the sake of advantage: flattering people who can benefit them
decisions.reason: θαυμάζοντες πρόσωπα, "admiring faces", is a Greek form of a Hebrew way of speaking of partiality, "lifting up the face" of someone, which the Law forbids in judgment (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17; compare James 2:1-9). ὠφελείας χάριν, "for the sake of advantage": they flatter those who can do something for them.

decisions.choice: flatter people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the idiom means here (m4).

decisions.choice: big, boastful words (B); brag with big words (R)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Peter 2:18 (m3).

L.18: that they were saying to you, "In [the] final time there will be scoffers, going according to their own desires for ungodly things."

R.17: But you, dear friends, must remember what the apostles of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} told you would happen.
R.18: They used to tell you, "In the last time, people will come who laugh and sneer. They will live by their own ungodly desires."

decisions.choice: one record: verse 18 says what the apostles' words were
alternatives: two records, divided at the raised dot after verse 17
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has a raised dot at the end of verse 17, but verse 18 begins with ὅτι, "that", which introduces the content of the words the readers are to remember. It cannot stand on its own as a sentence, so the two verses are one record, as 2 Peter 3:1-4 holds its parallel together.

decisions.choice: beloved: as in verse 3
decisions.reason: Jude turns from the false teachers to his readers, as he does again in verse 20.

decisions.choice: the apostles of our Lord: Jude speaks of them as others, whose words the readers had heard
decisions.reason: Jude does not count himself among the apostles. The readers had heard the apostles themselves: ἔλεγον, "they used to say", is an imperfect, which suggests a warning given more than once. Paul (Acts 20:29-30; 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:1-5) and Peter (2 Peter 3:3) gave such warnings.

decisions.choice: a saying of the apostles also found in 2 Peter 3:3
decisions.reason: 2 Peter 3:3 has nearly the same words: in the last days scoffers will come, going according to their own desires. Jude says "the last time" and adds "of ungodliness"; 2 Peter adds "with scoffing" and goes on to the scoffers' question about the Lord's coming. Both present it as something the readers had been told by the apostles.

decisions.choice: the last time: the time before the Lord's return, which Jude's readers were already living in
decisions.reason: The New Testament speaks of the last days or the last hour as already begun (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18). Verse 19 says of the false teachers, "These are" the scoffers: the warning is coming true.

decisions.choice: their own desires of ungodliness: desires for what is ungodly
decisions.reason: ἀσεβειῶν is plural, "ungodlinesses", a genitive that describes the desires: they want ungodly things. It is the word repeated in verse 15.

decisions.choice: dear friends
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

decisions.choice: people who laugh and sneer
decisions.reason: As in 2 Peter 3:3.

decisions.choice: a new sentence: They used to tell you
alternatives: that they used to say to you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable begin a new English sentence where the quotation is introduced; the meaning is the same (m1).

records.heading: Keep yourselves in God's love

records.source: οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ ἀποδιορίζοντες, ψυχικοί, πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες.
records.gloss: These are the [ones] causing divisions, natural [ones], spirit not having.
pieces: These people create divisions among you. They are worldly, and the Spirit is not in them.

L.19: These are the ones who cause divisions, natural [people], not having [the] Spirit.

R.19: These people split the church into groups. They think and act like the world around them, and they do not have God's Spirit.

decisions.choice: causing divisions: splitting the church into groups
alternatives: making distinctions, ranking people as more or less spiritual
decisions.reason: ἀποδιορίζω is found only here in the Bible. It means to mark off or divide. Most likely they create factions; some take it of drawing lines between supposedly spiritual and unspiritual believers, a claim Jude turns back on them in the next words.

decisions.choice: natural: living on the level of ordinary human life, without the Spirit
decisions.reason: ψυχικοί describes the person who has only natural human life, the life of the soul. Paul sets the natural person, who does not accept the things of the Spirit, against the spiritual person (1 Corinthians 2:14-15; compare 15:44-46), and James 3:15 uses the word for wisdom that is earthly. If the false teachers claimed to be the truly spiritual ones, Jude says the opposite.

decisions.choice: not having the Spirit: the Holy Spirit is not in them
alternatives: not having a spirit, a spiritual nature
decisions.reason: πνεῦμα has no article, but the contrast with "praying in the Holy Spirit" in the next verse shows that the Spirit of God is meant (compare Romans 8:9).

decisions.choice: natural (L); worldly (B); think and act like the world around them (R)
decisions.reason: "Natural" alone sounds like praise in current English. Balanced and Readable say what Jude means: their life belongs to this world and not to the Spirit (m2).

decisions.choice: God's Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable says whose Spirit is meant (m3).

records.source: ὑμεῖς δέ, ἀγαπητοί, ἐποικοδομοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ ὑμῶν πίστει, ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ προσευχόμενοι, ἑαυτοὺς ἐν ἀγάπῃ θεοῦ τηρήσατε προσδεχόμενοι τὸ ἔλεος τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον.
records.gloss: You but, beloved, building up yourselves on the most holy of you faith, in [the] Spirit Holy praying, \v 21 yourselves in [the] love of God keep, awaiting the mercy of the Lord of us Jesus Christ to life eternal.
pieces: But you, dear friends, keep building yourselves up on your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit.
Keep yourselves within God's love, while you look forward to the mercy of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} that brings eternal life.

L.20: But you, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in [the] Holy Spirit,
L.21: keep yourselves in [the] love of God, awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} to eternal life.

R.20: But you, dear friends, keep building your lives on your most holy faith. Pray as the Holy Spirit leads you and helps you.
R.21: Keep yourselves living in God's love. And look forward to the day when our Lord Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} will show you mercy and give you eternal life.

decisions.choice: one command, keep yourselves in God's love, with three participles that say how
decisions.reason: The only imperative is τηρήσατε, "keep". Building, praying and waiting describe how they are to do it, and they carry the force of commands too. Faith, the Holy Spirit, the love of God and the mercy of Jesus Christ: Jude's call names Father, Son and Spirit together.

decisions.choice: building yourselves up on your most holy faith: growing on the foundation of the faith handed on to you
decisions.reason: ἐποικοδομέω means to build on a foundation (1 Corinthians 3:10-14; Ephesians 2:20; Colossians 2:7). The faith here is what is believed, "handed over once for all" (verse 3), and it is most holy because it comes from God. "Yourselves" is plural: they build up one another as well as themselves.

decisions.choice: praying in the Holy Spirit: prayer led and empowered by the Spirit
decisions.reason: The Spirit helps believers pray (Romans 8:26-27; Ephesians 6:18). The words stand against verse 19: the false teachers do not have the Spirit, and the readers pray in him.

decisions.choice: the love of God: God's love for them, in which they are to remain
decisions.reason: ἀγάπῃ θεοῦ could mean God's love or love for God. Verse 1 calls them loved in God the Father, and the command is to keep themselves in that love, as Jesus said, "remain in my love" (John 15:9-10). So it most likely means God's love for them. Those who are kept (verse 1) are told to keep themselves: both are true.

decisions.choice: awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life: looking for the mercy he will show at his coming
decisions.reason: προσδέχομαι is eager expectation (Luke 2:25; Titus 2:13). The mercy is what Christ will show his people on the day of judgment (compare 2 Timothy 1:18), and its result is eternal life. "To eternal life" most likely goes with "mercy": mercy that brings them into eternal life.

decisions.choice: dear friends
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

decisions.choice: the participles as commands: keep building, pray, look forward
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the participles the force of commands, which they have here (m1).

decisions.choice: look forward to the day when our Lord Jesus Christ will show you mercy
alternatives: waiting for the mercy of our Lord
decisions.reason: Readable says when the mercy is shown, at the Lord's coming (m5).

decisions.choice: Pray as the Holy Spirit leads you and helps you
decisions.reason: Readable explains "in the Holy Spirit" (m3).

records.source: καὶ οὓς μὲν ἐλεᾶτε διακρινομένους, οὓς δὲ σῴζετε ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες, οὓς δὲ ἐλεᾶτε ἐν φόβῳ, μισοῦντες καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐσπιλωμένον χιτῶνα.
records.gloss: And some on one hand have mercy on, doubting [ones], \v 23 others but save out of fire snatching, others but have mercy on with fear, hating even the by the flesh having been stained tunic.
pieces: Be merciful to some who are wavering.
Save others by pulling them out of the fire. To still others show mercy, but with fear: hate even the clothes their sinful flesh has soiled.

L.22: And have mercy on some who doubt;
L.23: and save others, snatching [them] out of fire; and on others have mercy with fear, hating even the tunic stained by the flesh.

R.22: Show mercy to people who have doubts.
R.23: Pull others out of the fire and save them. Show mercy to still others, but do it with fear. Hate even the clothes that their sinful lives have made dirty.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: three groups: have mercy on some who doubt; save others, snatching them out of fire; have mercy on others with fear
alternatives: two groups, in a shorter text
"rebuke" or "convict" some who dispute, in place of the first "have mercy"
"have compassion on some, making a difference" (the reading the King James Version follows)
decisions.reason: These two verses are among the hardest in the New Testament to establish. The manuscripts differ in the number of groups (two or three), in the verbs (have mercy, rebuke or convict, save, snatch) and in their order. The SBLGNT prints a three-part text, with the verb ἐλεᾶτε, "have mercy", in the first and third parts and "save ... snatching" in the second. Some important manuscripts read "rebuke" or "convict" in the first part instead of "have mercy"; some, among them the early papyrus P72 and Codex Vaticanus, have a shorter text with only two groups; and the text behind the King James Version reads "have compassion on some, making a difference". In every form the readers are told to reach out to those in danger, some gently and some urgently, without sharing their sin. Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: who doubt: wavering, unsure, under the false teachers' influence
alternatives: who dispute, who argue with you
decisions.reason: διακρίνω in the middle voice can mean to doubt or waver (Matthew 21:21; James 1:6) or to dispute, as Michael disputed with the devil in verse 9. Here these people are to receive mercy, which fits those who are wavering better than those who argue.

decisions.choice: snatching them out of fire: rescuing people at the edge of judgment
decisions.reason: Amos 4:11 and Zechariah 3:2 speak of a burning stick snatched from the fire, someone rescued just in time; Zechariah 3:2 is also the verse Jude quotes in verse 9. The fire is the judgment of verse 7.

decisions.choice: with fear: with reverence toward God, and on guard against being drawn into their sin
decisions.reason: The fear is not fear of the people themselves. It is the awe of God that takes sin seriously, and the care of someone who knows that sin spreads (Galatians 6:1).

decisions.choice: hating even the tunic stained by the flesh: keep clear of every trace of their sin
decisions.reason: χιτῶνα is the tunic worn next to the skin. In Zechariah 3:3-4 Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments, which are taken away as a sign that his guilt is removed; it is the scene Jude has already drawn on in verse 9 and in "snatching them out of fire". ἐσπιλωμένον, "stained", is related to the word for a stain in 2 Peter 2:13. "The flesh" is human nature as sin uses it (verses 7-8). Mercy goes out to the person; hatred is for the sin, even for what has touched it.

decisions.choice: tunic (L); clothes (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal names the garment; Balanced and Readable use the ordinary word, since the point is what the clothing has touched (m5).

decisions.choice: their sinful flesh (B); their sinful lives (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whose flesh, and in what sense (m5).

decisions.choice: who doubt (L); who are wavering (B); who have doubts (R)
decisions.reason: All three render the sense chosen in m2.

records.source: Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ φυλάξαι ὑμᾶς ἀπταίστους καὶ στῆσαι κατενώπιον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ ἀμώμους ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει μόνῳ θεῷ σωτῆρι ἡμῶν διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν δόξα μεγαλωσύνη κράτος καὶ ἐξουσία πρὸ παντὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς πάντας τοὺς αἰῶνας· ἀμήν.
records.gloss: To the [one] now being able to guard you without stumbling and to make stand before the glory of him blameless with exultation, \v 25 to only God Savior of us through Jesus Christ the Lord of us, glory, majesty, might and authority, before all the age and now and into all the ages; amen.
pieces: Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling, and to bring you into the presence of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory without blemish and rejoicing greatly,
to God alone, our Savior, through Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, before time began, now, and for all the ages to come. Amen.

L.24: Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling and to make [you] stand before {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory without blemish, in exultation,
L.25: to God alone, our Savior, through Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} our Lord, [be] glory, majesty, might, and authority, before all the age, and now, and into all the ages. Amen.

R.24: God is able to guard you, so that you do not stumble and fall. He can bring you into {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glorious presence without any fault, and you will be filled with gladness.
R.25: He is the only God, our Savior. Through Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} our Lord, may glory, greatness, power, and authority be {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, before time began, now, and forever! Amen.

decisions.choice: one record: the doxology and its closing Amen
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has a raised dot before ἀμήν, "Amen". The Amen cannot stand alone: it is the closing response to the doxology, as in 2 Peter 3:18, and the record keeps it with the doxology.

decisions.choice: a doxology: glory is ascribed to God, and the verb is understood
decisions.reason: There is no verb. In such words of praise the sense is a wish or an acclamation: may glory be his, or glory is his (Romans 16:25-27; 2 Peter 3:18). The opening lines describe God by what he is able to do.

decisions.choice: without stumbling, without blemish: kept from falling, and presented faultless
decisions.reason: ἀπταίστους means not stumbling: not falling into sin or away from the faith, the opposite of what has happened to the false teachers. ἀμώμους is the word for a sacrifice without defect (1 Peter 1:19) and for the people God presents to himself (Ephesians 1:4; Colossians 1:22). The verb for guarding, φυλάσσω, is not the "keep" of verses 1 and 21 but a word for guarding or protecting.

decisions.choice: to make you stand before his glory: to bring you into God's presence on the last day
decisions.reason: κατενώπιον means in the very presence of. God's glory stands for God himself in his splendor; to stand before it is to be welcomed on the day of judgment, not condemned. ἀγαλλιάσει is exultant joy, the gladness of a festival.

decisions.choice: the only God our Savior: God himself is Savior, and he saves through Jesus Christ
decisions.reason: Calling God "Savior" is common in the Old Testament (Isaiah 43:3, 11; 45:21) and in the New (Luke 1:47; 1 Timothy 1:1; Titus 1:3). "Only" confesses that there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). Verse 4 used "only" of Jesus Christ as Master; Jude sets the two side by side without explaining how they relate.

decisions.choice: through Jesus Christ our Lord: most likely with the praise: glory is given to God through Christ
alternatives: with "Savior": God saves through Jesus Christ
decisions.reason: The phrase stands between "our Savior" and the list of praises. Elsewhere glory is given to God through Jesus Christ (Romans 16:27; 1 Peter 4:11), and that is the most likely sense here; it can also be read with "Savior", and both are true.

decisions.choice: glory, majesty, might, authority: God's splendor, greatness, power and right to rule
decisions.reason: Glory (δόξα) is God's honor and splendor; majesty (μεγαλωσύνη) is his greatness (Hebrews 1:3; 8:1); might (κράτος) is his ruling power; authority (ἐξουσία) is his right to rule.

decisions.choice: before all the age, and now, and into all the ages: for all time, past, present and future
decisions.reason: πρὸ παντὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος means before all time. Jude's doxology reaches back before creation as well as forward without end.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "the only God", with "through Jesus Christ our Lord" and "before all time"
alternatives: "the only wise God" (the reading the King James Version follows)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "wise" after "only" (compare Romans 16:27) and leave out "through Jesus Christ our Lord" and "before all time"; the King James Version follows that text. The SBLGNT follows the earlier manuscripts, which have the longer phrases and lack "wise". Reviewers must check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: guard
decisions.reason: "Keep" is kept for the verb of verses 1, 6, 13 and 21; this is a different verb (m3).

decisions.choice: God alone (L, B); the only God (R)
decisions.reason: "To God alone" and "the only God" say the same: there is no other God (m5).

decisions.choice: God is able
decisions.reason: Readable names God at once, as verse 25 does.

decisions.choice: before time began, now, and for all the ages to come (B); before time began, now, and forever (R)
alternatives: before all the age, and now, and into all the ages
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say the same span of time in current English (m8).

decisions.choice: you will be filled with gladness
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly whose joy is meant: the joy of those God brings before him (m4).
